item.title: Modular fault-tolerant quantum computing on a non-CSS code
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Realized complete set of modular fault-tolerant logical operations for the non-CSS [[5,1,3]] code on a 16-qubit trapped-ion processor, including state teleportation, QEC with real-time feedback, and magic-state injection yielding 85±8% average gate fidelity for a logical T gate.

Grade 0.515 · 3.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Robert Freund, Friederike Butt, César Benito, Ivan Pogorelov, Marcel Meyer, Alex Steiner, Alejandro Bermudez, Markus Müller, Thomas Monz

Figure

Magic-state preparation circuit and quantum process tomography of the non-Clifford logical T gate injection, showing reconstructed logical Pauli transfer matrix elements and process fidelity.

Asks

Can universal modular fault-tolerant quantum operations, including inter-register state teleportation and non-Clifford gate injection, be realized experimentally on a compact non-CSS quantum error-correcting code?

Before

Logical teleportation and lattice-surgery primitives had previously been demonstrated only on topological Calderbank–Shor–Steane (CSS) codes (such as surface and color codes).

But

State preparation uses postselection on syndrome verification flags; SPAM-error removal method requires trace-preserving noise channels and is restricted to operations without error-detection postselection.

Tools

16-qubit linear Paul trap (⁴⁰Ca⁺ ions) · non-CSS $[[5, 1, 3]]$ code · real-time mid-circuit measurement and feedback · logical Pauli process tomography

Abstract

Modularization promises to break down the design and implementation complexity of large scale quantum processors into smaller manageable subtasks. In this approach, quantum channels, realized for instance through physical rerouting of qubits or quantum teleportation, connect multiple modules. Each of those modules hosts a subset of qubits, e.g. multiple logical qubits, and provides quantum operations on them. In this work, we implement for the first time all logical operations required for modular fault-tolerant universal quantum computing with a non-Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) code, the perfect $[[5, 1, 3]]$ code, on a trapped-ion quantum computer. This code is the smallest quantum error-correcting (QEC) code capable of correcting any single-qubit error, making it a compact alternative to larger CSS codes. We demonstrate logical state teleportation and a full suite of fault-tolerant operations required for universal logical control, including logical state preparation, QEC with real-time feedback, logical measurements, magic-state preparation, logical entangling operations, and magic-state injection. Moreover, we characterize the logical spectator error picked up by idling logical qubits during quantum operations on distinct qubit registers and demonstrate a logical Pauli quantum process tomography that minimizes required sampling resources for logical tomography.

item.title: Flow-Based Lattice Surgery Optimization with Runtime T Gate Scheduling
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Jointly compiles Clifford routing via maximum-flow and runtime magic state cultivation in a 3D topological pipe diagram, cutting spacetime volume by 2.3× (geometric mean) and running 10.8× faster than TopoLS under free magic states, and cutting volume by 2.3× at code distance d=13 relative to PureMagic.

Grade 0.446 · 3.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “lattice surgery, logical qubit layout and compilation to a fault-tolerant instr…” · Raymond Iacobacci, Tianyi Hao, Neer Patel, Siyuan Niu

Figure

Execution latency per logical cycle compared between PureMagic and FlowRouter across circuit benchmarks, showing runtime dispatch speed relative to surface code cycle times.

Asks

How can topological lattice surgery compilation simultaneously embed full circuit layers of Clifford operations and account for stochastic, in-place magic state cultivation in a single 3D representation?

Before

TopoLS routes Clifford gates sequentially or via MCTS order search while omitting magic state preparation footprints; PureMagic schedules cultivation on a 2D layout with per-instruction path search.

But

Evaluated on rotated surface codes with distances d=11,13,15; volume advantage drops to 1.6× at d=15 where expected cultivation time rises to 5.5 logical cycles.

Tools

ZX-calculus · 3D topological pipe diagrams · Maximum-flow formulation · Magic state cultivation (MSC) · Runtime delay mechanisms

Abstract

Lattice surgery on the surface code is a leading route to fault-tolerant quantum computation. Compiling logical circuits into lattice surgery operations is a pivotal step that determines the resource cost of a computation. Prior compilers build on idealized assumptions, and one that works in practical settings remains to be developed. Existing works are either unscalable or route one gate at a time within a layer, so the embedding depends on the order of gates and opportunities to route many gates at once are lost. In addition, they assume magic states are always available and cost-free, even though preparing one costs more than a Clifford operation. We present FlowRouter, the first topological lattice surgery compiler that places Clifford routing and stochastic magic state cultivation inside a single 3D embedding. At compile time, FlowRouter formulates the routing of an entire circuit layer as a maximum-flow problem, embedding many gates simultaneously. At runtime, it allows magic states to be cultivated at every idling patch, works with the realistic cultivation process with multiplexing and multi-stage post-selections, and absorbs the stochasticity by introducing delay mechanisms that add as little spacetime volume as possible. With magic states assumed free, FlowRouter reduces spacetime volume by 2.3x and compiles 10.8x faster than the state-of-the-art static topological lattice surgery compiler. With the cultivation-aware setting that includes both Clifford and magic state cost, FlowRouter reduces spacetime volume by 2.3x on a distance-13 surface code when compared with the state-of-the-art runtime compiler.

item.title: Quantum Hashing with QKD States
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Constructed quantum hash function mapping n-bit inputs to k=⌈n/2⌉+O(log2⁡n) single-qubit BB84 states, achieving collision threshold F(ψC)≤1/(2n) from shortened binary BCH codes.

Grade 0.436 · 2.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “quantum LDPC codes and low-overhead fault tolerance” · A. V. Vasiliev, I. G. Zinnatullin

Asks

Can quantum hashing be implemented on existing commercial QKD hardware using standard BB84 states?

But

Requires n=32 or n≥44 to guarantee output qubit compression k<n.

Tools

binary linear error-correcting codes · narrow-sense BCH codes · code shortening · BB84 quantum states

Abstract

Quantum hashing is a well-known technique. In this paper, we present a new construction of a quantum hash function based on binary error-correcting codes. The construction of the quantum hash strongly resembles the quantum state preparation in QKD protocols (e.g., BB84 protocol) and can be implemented on current QKD-devices.

item.title: Simultaneous Reduction of Observables and Measured Qudits in Entanglement-Assisted Quantum Local Recovery
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Linear algebraic algorithm with complexity O(|K|3) computes a reduced repair group J⊆K of codeword qudits and a set of observables O of strictly minimal size |O|=dim⁡πI(C⟂s) to locally recover erasures at positions I⊊K.

Grade 0.419 · 2.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum Low-Density Parity-Check Codes” · Ryutaroh Matsumoto

Asks

How can one simultaneously reduce both the number of measured observables and the number of measured codeword qudits in local recovery for general entanglement-assisted quantum error-correcting codes?

Before

Simultaneous reduction was limited to unassisted quantum stabilizer codes from Hermitian dual-containing linear codes (Matsumoto 2024), without methods for general entanglement-assisted codes or general CSS codes.

But

Computed set of observables is provably minimal, but reduced repair group J is not guaranteed to achieve globally minimal size.

Tools

symplectic inner products · punctured and shortened codes · linear subspace decomposition · greedy column reduction

Abstract

For a general entanglement-assisted or unassisted quantum error-correcting code, a set of erasures, and an associated repair group, we propose a linear algebraic procedure to compute a reduced set of observables and a reduced repair group of codeword qudits for correcting the given erasures. The procedure has cubic complexity in the repair group size and the computed set of observables has the smallest possible size for correcting the given erasures. We specialize the general procedure to quantum codes constructed from Euclidean and Hermitian orthogonality, and provide closed-form upper bounds on the size of reduced repair groups for those special cases. Based on these closed-form bounds, we propose quantum counterparts of the information locality of classical local recovery.

item.title: A thermal microwave bus for neutral atom quantum computing
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Bichromatic Raman gate mediating interaction via a 3D microwave cavity virtually populates Rydberg states and cancels dispersive shifts, reaching gate fidelity F=0.997.

Grade 0.414 · 2.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Surface codes: Towards practical large-scale quantum computation” · Matthew J. H. Kendall, Christopher J. Watson, Michael Ben Shem, Jonathan D. Breeze

Figure

Error-correction round time plotted against code distance d for the toric code and gross code, comparing purely shuttling-based qubit movement with the hybrid cavity-bus scheme.

Asks

Can microwave cavity-mediated entangling gates overcome the shuttling-time bottleneck and thermal sensitivity in neutral-atom arrays at finite cryogenic temperatures?

Before

was 0.76 for optical cavity deterministic CZ gates (Steiner 2023)

But

Numerical open-system simulations of up to 4 atoms, analytical Magnus-expansion bounds, requires cryogenic temperatures (T≲1 K) and high-Q cavity (Q>109).

Tools

3D re-entrant microwave cavity · Open quantum system Lindblad simulations · Schrieffer-Wolff perturbation theory · Optical tweezer array

Abstract

High-fidelity two-qubit gates in neutral-atom arrays rely on the Rydberg blockade, which is intrinsically short ranged and requires long range connectivity to be achieved through atom shuttling. We propose a four level architecture, where the typical ground state qubit can be leveraged for its long lifetime and the Rydberg states couple to a microwave cavity, allowing for long range cavity mediated gates. We first find the thermal dependence of two established protocols, the dispersive iSWAP native to the Tavis-Cummings model and the Controlled phase gate generated from driving the cavity. We simulate them under the presence of Rydberg decay, thermal photons, finite cavity linewidth and find fidelities which accompany closed form bounds. We then introduce the bichromatic Raman gate, which only virtually populates the Rydberg states and cancels dispersive shifts to mitigate both atomic and cavity decay, achieving a fidelity of F = 0.997. Finally, we consider a full optical tweezer array in a microwave cavity, and show that using a cavity mediated gate to close the periodic boundaries of the toric code shortens an error correction round by a factor of 2.3 for realistic array sizes. This was then applied to the wider family of Bivariate bicycle codes, and we find that it shortens a round of the gross code by a factor of 4.8.

item.title: Metric Self-Dual Completion and Optimal Additive Hardness for Quantum and Graph-State Distance
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — NP-hard to approximate quantum code distance and graph-state distance within additive error $c N$ for constant c>0, via deterministic reductions.

Grade 0.391 · 2.3σ above the day's baseline · matched “How to factor 2048 bit RSA integers in 8 hours using 20 million noisy qubits” · Rafail Ostrovsky

Asks

Does quantum-code distance or graph-state distance admit a linear additive hardness gap under deterministic reductions?

Before

Additive hardness gap was N1/2 for quantum code distance (Kapshikar and Kundu 2023; Grigorescu et al. 2024) and N1/3 for graph-state distance (Grigorescu et al. 2024).

But

CSS codes with identical X- and Z-check spaces, constant rate, and constant relative distance. Does not establish hardness for quantum LDPC codes.

Tools

Metric self-dual completion · Prefix-sum construction · Deterministic Karp reductions · Dual-good to self-dual conversion

Abstract

We prove that the quantum code distance is NP-hard to approximate within an additive error of $c N$, for some constant c >0, where N is the number of qubits. Our reductions are deterministic. This improves the previous square-root additive gap to Ω(N) and resolves the explicitly stated linear-gap question of Kapshikar and Kundu. Our result holds for CSS codes with identical X- and Z-check spaces, and with a constant rate and constant relative distance. For every fixed λ>1, there is a constant c>0 such that hardness still holds even when every nonidentity stabilizer has weight greater than λ times the quantum distance. We also improve the hardness gap of graph state distance on N vertices of Grigorescu, Jha, and Samperton from cube-root to Ω(N), resolving their explicitly stated open question. Both hardness results are asymptotically optimal since both distances are at most N. Our graph state distance hardness result holds for balanced bipartite graphs with a binary adjacency matrix that is its own inverse (mod 2). Our main technique for both hardness bounds above is classical: we show how to convert any code C of length m into a self-dual code A(C) of length N=Θ(m) while exactly doubling the original coset metric. The conversion is deterministic and efficient. We call it the metric self-dual completion of C. It comes with a linear embedding τ: F₂^m hookrightarrowF₂^N. The embedding doubles all Hamming distances between vectors in F₂^m and all pairwise distances between corresponding cosets. The embedding also guarantees that all codewords of A(C) of weight at most 2m are exactly τ(C).

item.title: Resource and entanglement study of a hybrid qudit-qubit quantum algorithm for solving the integer programming problem
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Hybrid qudit-qubit integer programming reduces fault-tolerant resource requirements by ∼180× for qutrits (d=3) and ∼2220× for ququints (d=5) compared to qubit-only implementation.

Grade 0.379 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “quantum LDPC codes and low-overhead fault tolerance” · Kapil Goswami, Rick Mukherjee, Peter Schmelcher

Figure

Reduced-state entropy S(A) plotted against subsystem dimension ⟨log2⁡(dim⁡A)⟩ across algorithm stages for dimensions d=2,3,4, showing volume-law-like scaling up to the Page saturation limit.

Asks

What is the quantitative resource advantage of a hybrid qudit-qubit quantum algorithm over qubit-only encoding, and is it classically simulable based on its entanglement structure?

But

Simplified fault-tolerant resource counting model, numerical evaluations limited to d≤5 and small system sizes, classical hardness inferred via scaling bounds rather than rigorous simulation runtime proofs.

Tools

Fault-tolerant surface code resource estimation · Magic-state distillation scaling · von Neumann entropy and Schmidt rank tracking · Multipartite mutual information analysis · Matrix Product State classical simulation bounds

Abstract

Recently, a hybrid qudit-qubit algorithm [1] was presented for solving the integer programming problem with a polynomial quantum advantage. In this work, we investigate the algorithm [1] to understand the role of qudits (d-dimensional quantum system) by conducting a comparative resource analysis with its qubit-only implementation and the classical simulability of the algorithm by exploring the entanglement structure. The resource analysis part is performed in terms of logical gate counts, and fault-tolerant physical resources, including non-Clifford gates. The hybrid qudit-qubit implementation has a more compact structure of the unitary operators as opposed to its qubit-only simulation which reduces the logical and fault-tolerant resource requirements. Two example problems, one with qutrits (d=3) and the other with ququint (d=5), when contrasted with their qubit-only implementation, within a simplified fault-tolerant resource model, showed ∼180 × and ∼2220× fewer total resource count, respectively. For the entanglement study, volume-law-like entropy growth and signatures of multi-partite entanglement is observed leading to increasing difficulty in the classical simulation of the algorithm. The algorithm generates synergistic tri-partite entanglement even for a quadratic problem, revealing that the algorithmic structure itself can generate higher-order entanglement in the system independent of the problem.

item.title: Universality in Terms of The BECs Bloch-Sphere Manipulations
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — Formulates Controlled-Bloch-Sphere Universality (CBSU) for (N+1)-dimensional SU(2) BEC qubit systems across Fock-basis and coherent-state representations. Proves an analogue of Gottesman-Knill theorem for BEC circuits composed of Stokes-Hermite Clifford gates and Fock basis measurements.

Grade 0.379 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “Fault-tolerant quantum computation by anyons” · Genji Fujii

Asks

How can universal quantum computation and the Gottesman-Knill theorem be formulated for Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) qubit systems spanning (N+1)-dimensional SU(2) representations?

But

Excludes distorted Bloch spheres caused by errors. Assumes Fock states can be fully manipulated as qudits without specifying experimental physical implementations.

Tools

Stokes operators · BEC coherent states · Gottesman-Knill theorem extension · Controlled-Bloch-Sphere Universality (CBSU)

Abstract

Quantum computing promises to outperform classical computing for certain computational tasks. One of the key concepts underlying this potential is universality. Universality has been extensively studied not only for qubits but also for higher-dimensional quantum systems, such as qutrits and qudits, which span Hilbert spaces of dimension greater than two. However, the concept of universality in Bose-Einstein condensates (BECs) qubit systems, which have been proposed relatively recently, remains insufficiently understood. In this work, we analyzed universality in BECs qubit systems. Our results clarify the theoretical aspects of universality in quantum computation within the class of ((N+1))-dimensional representations of SU(2), taking into account two distinct representations of the quantum states.
